extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and researchers in functional analysis (Banach space theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and key properties about weak and weak* topologies, reflexive and separable Banach spaces, and uniform convexity. Useful as a checklist of facts/criteria to use when reasoning about compactness, convergence, continuity, and minimization in Banach-space contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: weak topology σ(E, E*)
rubrics_metrics.description: The weak topology σ(E, E*) on E is the coarsest topology making all elements of E* (continuous linear functionals) continuous; neighborhoods are generated by finitely many evaluations (Proposition 3.4 / construction in Section 3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basis neighborhoods: sets of the form {x ∈ E; |⟨f_i, x - x0⟩| < ε, i =1..k} for finite collections f_i ∈ E*. Use this when checking weak continuity or weak convergence (pointwise convergence of functionals). Note: weak topology is coarser than the norm (strong) topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak topology is coarser than strong topology; more compact sets
rubrics_metrics.description: σ(E, E*) has fewer open (resp. closed) sets than the strong (norm) topology; coarser topologies tend to have more compact sets (Remarks 8, 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle when looking for compactness: e.g., sets non-compact in strong topology may be compact in weak topology (motivates Banach–Alaoglu). Do not confuse coarser topology with same convergence patterns in infinite dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: unit ball never weakly open in infinite-dimensional E
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is infinite-dimensional the open unit ball U = {x ∈ E; ||x|| < 1} is never open in the weak topology σ(E, E*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using that complement would be weakly closed and intersect with unit sphere; illustrates difference between weak and strong topologies and shows weak topology is strictly coarser in infinite dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remark: weak topology not metrizable in infinite dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: In infinite-dimensional spaces the weak topology σ(E, E*) is never metrizable (Remark 3); no metric or norm on E induces the weak topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to use metric-sequence/compactness equivalences on whole E under the weak topology unless you restrict to bounded sets and have separability/metrizability hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.7: convex sets — weakly closed iff strongly closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Let C be a convex subset of E. Then C is closed in the weak topology σ(E, E*) if and only if it is closed in the strong (norm) topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Hahn–Banach separation to show complements are weakly open. Consequence: for convex sets, checking strong closedness suffices to infer weak closedness; conversely, weak closed convex sets are strongly closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3.8 (Mazur): convex combinations yield strong limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n → x weakly, then there exists a sequence y_n of convex combinations of the x_n's that converges strongly (in norm) to x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tool: to pass from weak convergence to strong convergence in approximation arguments, replace sequences by convex combinations (useful in optimization and variational problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3.9: convex and strongly l.s.c. ⇒ weakly l.s.c.
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ : E → (−∞, +∞] is convex and lower semicontinuous (l.s.c.) in the strong topology, then φ is l.s.c. in the weak topology σ(E, E*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by verifying sublevel sets are convex and strongly closed, then use Theorem 3.7. Example: the norm function x ↦ ||x|| is weakly l.s.c.; consequence: weak limits satisfy ||x|| ≤ lim inf ||x_n||.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.10: continuity of linear operators (strong ↔ weak)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let T: E → F be linear between Banach spaces. T is continuous in the strong topologies iff it is continuous from E weak σ(E, E*) into F weak σ(F, F*), and conversely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For linear maps, continuity notions S→S, W→W, S→W are equivalent; however W→S is rare and requires finite-dimensional range (see Remark 7). Use closed-graph theorem on the graph in product weak topology to deduce strong continuity from weak continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remark: few linear operators are W→S continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear operator is continuous from weak to strong iff it is continuous S→S and additionally has finite-dimensional range (dim R(T) < ∞) (Remark 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume weak→strong continuity except in these restrictive situations; this is a common pitfall in nonlinear analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: weak* topology σ(E*, E)
rubrics_metrics.description: The weak* topology σ(E*, E) on the dual E* is the coarsest topology making all evaluation maps f ↦ ⟨f, x⟩ (x ∈ E) continuous; neighborhoods are given by finitely many evaluations (Proposition 3.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working in E* treat convergence f_n → f in σ(E*, E) as pointwise convergence on E: ⟨f_n, x⟩ → ⟨f, x⟩ for all x ∈ E (Proposition 3.13(i)). Use basis V(x1,..,xk; ε) described in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3.13: characterizing weak* convergence and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (f_n) in E* converges to f in σ(E*, E) iff ⟨f_n, x⟩ → ⟨f, x⟩ for all x ∈ E. If f_n → f strongly then f_n → f weak*, and boundedness and liminf inequality for norms hold under weak* convergence (boundedness of norms and ||f|| ≤ lim inf ||f_n||).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pointwise tests for weak* convergence. Note: strong convergence implies weak* convergence, but not conversely; weak* convergence still controls norm via liminf inequality and boundedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3.14: weak*-continuous linear functionals on E* are evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: Every linear functional ϕ on E* that is continuous for σ(E*, E) has the form ϕ(f) = ⟨f, x0⟩ for some x0 ∈ E (Proposition 3.14, proof via Lemma 3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: hyperplanes closed in σ(E*, E) are of evaluation form (Corollary 3.15). Useful to identify weak* closed sets and to characterize dual-space topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.16 (Banach–Alaoglu–Bourbaki): weak* compactness of dual ball
rubrics_metrics.description: The closed unit ball B_{E*} = {f ∈ E*; ||f|| ≤ 1} is compact in the weak* topology σ(E*, E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: view E* as subset of R^E with product topology and apply Tychonoff; use algebraic constraints to get closed subset. This is fundamental to existence arguments (e.g., minimization, weak-* sequential compactness on metrizable subsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: reflexive Banach space (canonical injection surjective)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Banach space E is reflexive if the canonical injection J: E → E** is surjective, i.e., J(E) = E** (definition at start of Section 3.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice identify E with its double dual when reflexive. Finite-dimensional, L^p (1<p<∞), and Hilbert spaces are reflexive; L^1, L^∞, C(K) typically are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.17 (Kakutani): reflexivity ⇔ unit ball weakly compact
rubrics_metrics.description: E is reflexive iff the closed unit ball B_E is compact in the weak topology σ(E, E*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Banach–Alaoglu on double dual and continuity of J to get one direction; conversely use Goldstine and density arguments to deduce surjectivity of J. This provides a practical compactness criterion for reflexivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3.3 (Helly): equivalence for approximate interpolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f1,..,fk ∈ E* and γ1,..,γk ∈ R, condition (i) existence of x_ε with ||x_ε|| ≤1 with |⟨f_i, x_ε⟩ - γ_i| < ε for all i (approximate solvability) is equivalent to (ii) inequality |Σ β_i γ_i| ≤ ||Σ β_i f_i|| for all β ∈ R^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Helly lemma to relate moment/interpolation approximations on unit ball to dual-norm inequalities. Useful technical tool in density/compactness proofs (e.g., Goldstine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3.4 (Goldstine): density of J(B_E) in B_{E**}
rubrics_metrics.description: For any Banach space E, J(B_E) is dense in B_{E**} with respect to the weak** topology σ(E**, E*). Consequently J(E) is weak** dense in E**.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used in the converse direction of Kakutani and shows that double dual unit ball can be approximated by images of primal unit ball; important in duality and reflexivity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.18: bounded sequences in reflexive spaces have weakly convergent subsequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is reflexive and (x_n) is a bounded sequence in E, then there exists a subsequence that converges in the weak topology σ(E, E*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a compactness-type consequence of reflexivity (B_E weakly compact). Use when extracting weak limits from bounded sequences in reflexive spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.19 (Eberlein–Šmulian): sequence-compactness criterion for reflexivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If every bounded sequence in E admits a weakly convergent subsequence (in σ(E, E*)), then E is reflexive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a sequential characterization: weak sequential compactness of bounded sets implies reflexivity. The proof is delicate (reference provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3.20: closed subspace of reflexive space is reflexive
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is reflexive and M ⊂ E is a closed linear subspace, then M (with norm from E) is reflexive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equality of weak topologies induced on M (Hahn–Banach) and Theorem 3.17. Useful when checking reflexivity of naturally occurring subspaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3.21: reflexivity equivalence for dual
rubrics_metrics.description: A Banach space E is reflexive iff its dual space E* is reflexive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use canonical identifications and dualization: reflexivity passes back and forth between E and E*.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3.22: bounded closed convex subsets in reflexive spaces are weakly compact
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is reflexive and K ⊂ E is bounded, closed and convex, then K is compact in the weak topology σ(E, E*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine Theorem 3.7 (convex closed sets) and Theorem 3.17. Apply to existence problems where compactness is required on convex feasible sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3.23: existence of minimizer for convex l.s.c. coercive functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is reflexive and A ⊂ E nonempty closed convex, and φ: A → (−∞,∞] is convex, l.s.c., not identically +∞ and coercive (φ(x) → +∞ as ||x||→∞ when A unbounded), then φ attains a minimum on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: sublevel sets are closed, convex, bounded hence weakly compact; φ is weakly l.s.c. by Corollary 3.9, so minimum exists. Use in variational calculus and optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.24: duality for densely defined closed operators in reflexive spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E and F be reflexive Banach spaces and A: D(A)⊂E→F a densely defined closed linear operator. Then D(A*) is dense in F* and A** = A (i.e., double-adjoint equals A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful structural fact when working with unbounded operators in reflexive settings; relies on reflexivity to identify double adjoint domain and closure properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: separable metric space and basic permanence (Proposition 3.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space E is separable if it has a countable dense subset. Every subset of a separable metric space is separable (Proposition 3.25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use separability to get countable approximations and to construct metrics/norms producing metrizability on bounded sets. Subset-separability used in arguments restricting to spans of sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.26: E* separable ⇒ E separable
rubrics_metrics.description: If E* is separable then E is separable (construction via dense sequence in E* and associated vectors in E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note converse false in general (e.g., E = L^1 is separable but E* = L^∞ is not). Use when deducing primal separability from dual separability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3.27: separable + reflexive equivalence between E and E*
rubrics_metrics.description: [E reflexive and separable] ⇔ [E* reflexive and separable].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine previous reflexivity and separability theorems to infer dual properties; helpful when checking metrizability or compactness on unit balls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.28: metrizability of B_{E*} ↔ separability of E
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is separable then B_{E*} is metrizable in σ(E*, E). Conversely, if B_{E*} is metrizable in σ(E*, E) then E is separable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric construction uses a countable dense subset of B_E to define a norm [·] producing a metric on B_{E*}. Use to reduce compactness to sequential compactness on metrizable unit balls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.29: metrizability of B_E ↔ separability of E*
rubrics_metrics.description: If E* is separable then the closed unit ball B_E is metrizable in the weak topology σ(E, E*). Conversely, if B_E is metrizable in σ(E, E*) then E* is separable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dual statement to Theorem 3.28. Use when you want to get sequential compactness properties for sequences in E via metrizability of B_E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3.30: weak* sequential compactness in separable primal
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is separable and (f_n) is a bounded sequence in E*, then there exists a subsequence converging in the weak* topology σ(E*, E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply because B_{E*} is compact and metrizable under separability of E (Theorems 3.16 and 3.28); gives sequential compactness for bounded sequences in dual when primal separable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: uniformly convex Banach space
rubrics_metrics.description: E is uniformly convex if ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 such that for x,y with ||x|| ≤ 1, ||y|| ≤ 1 and ||x-y|| > ε we have ||(x+y)/2|| < 1 − δ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: unit ball is uniformly 'round' (no long flat segments on sphere). Consequences include reflexivity and uniqueness of best approximations. Examples: ℝ^2 with Euclidean norm (ℓ2) is uniformly convex; ℓ1 and ℓ∞ are not. Use definition when proving strong geometric/compactness properties.
